Recently, a Chinese friend told me something that caught my attention. He needed to deal with a local government department. He simply accessed a community service through Weixin (the mainland Chinese version of WeChat). He told me how much of his daily life is connected to the app, from payments and shopping to transport and public services. That conversation got me thinking. Tencent's biggest advantage isn't just its technology. It's the habit of millions of people relying on its ecosystem every day. That kind of network effect is difficult to replace. And yet, the share price has fallen nearly 39% from its October 2025 peak. Has the business really lost that much value? I don't think so. AI Is Already Helping Tencent's Existing Business What interests me isn't another AI story built on future promises. Tencent already has a profitable ecosystem, and AI is helping it make better use of that network. In 2Q2026, advertising revenue grew 22%, supported by AI-powered recommendations. Group revenue rose 11%, while adjusted net profit grew 9%. The concern is that AI investments are costly and may take time to pay off. Fair enough. But I believe Tencent has an advantage: it can apply AI to existing services rather than having to build an audience from scratch. Market Take | The AI Panic Is Over? Wall Street's Buy-the-Dip Calls Send Chip Stocks Flying
Semiconductors Stage a Massive Rebound
The $PHLX Semiconductor Index (.SOX.US)$ surged 6.9% on Monday, recovering part of last week's 12%+ selloff as investors reassessed fears of tighter AI infrastructure regulation following the Democratic midterm victories.
$Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.US)$ jumped 13.3%, $Broadcom (AVGO.US)$ gained 8.8%, while $NVIDIA (NVDA.US)$ fell 4.2% amid separate CEO-related concerns. The rebound suggests investors are increasingly viewing the data center regulatory scare as an overreaction rather than a fundamental reset of the AI investment cycle.
Wall Street Is Buying the Dip, but Views Remain Divided
Several major institutions have pushed back against last week's panic:
– $Morgan Stanley (MS.US)$ : Called the selloff overdone and recommended buying the dip. It expects around 5GW of data center projects to shift from 2028 to 2029, rather than be canceled, with 2027 projects largely unaffected.
– $UBS Group (UBS.US)$ : Sees the selloff as a de-risking event rather than a deterioration in fundamentals. Regulation may delay or relocate projects, but underlying AI demand remains intact.
– $HSBC Holdings (HSBC.US)$ : Is increasing equity exposure following the correction, particularly in U.S. and Asian technology stocks. It sees Anthropic's anticipated IPO as a key near-term catalyst.
– $Jefferies Financial (JEF.US)$ : Called the November 5 selloff reactionary rather than a fundamental reset. Its historical analysis shows that S&P 500 declines exceeding 4% have been followed by average gains of 11.9% over six months and more than 20% over 12 months.
– $Oppenheimer Holdings (OPY.US)$ : Upgraded $Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.US)$ to Outperform with a $600 price target, forecasting 135% data center revenue growth in 2027. It sees incremental political risks to data center construction emerging mainly from 2H28.
– $Goldman Sachs (GS.US)$ : Expects potential data center moratoriums to be relatively short-lived. Its FICC team also noted that data center stocks had fallen 36% from their highs, memory stocks 42%, optical networking 46%, and neoclouds 57%, leaving valuations significantly reset.
– $State Street (STT.US)$ Investment Management: Believes the election accelerated an AI correction that was already underway, without fundamentally changing the long-term AI investment thesis.
– $JPMorgan (JPM.US)$ Asset Management: Remains more cautious about the 2028 buildout. Its Michael Cembalest estimates that 37.5GW of planned 2028 capacity could face construction pauses, with another 15GW subject to additional conditions. Most 2027 projects are less exposed.
– $Citigroup (C.US)$ : Downgraded U.S. equities and global technology from Overweight to Neutral, warning that investor positioning could deteriorate further before sentiment stabilizes.
– Aletheia Capital: Stood out as a single-stock bear, downgrading Nvidia to Hold from Buy and removing its $340 price target, citing growing financial commitments tied to Nvidia's AI Computing Partner program.
What History Says About SOX Below Its 250-Day Average
Historical data provide a more cautious perspective. Across 55 completed instances of SOX crossing below its 250-day moving average since October 2007, the median return was +0.57% over the following five trading days, with 54.5% of instances ending higher. Over 20 trading days, the median return improved to +1.36% , with 56.4% of instances posting gains. However, over 60 trading days, the median return turned negative at -3.43% , with only 41.8% of instances ending higher.
Interestingly, the average 60-day return was still positive at +0.83% , suggesting that a handful of strong rebounds skewed the average. The negative median and sub-50% win rate point to a less favorable medium-term historical pattern.
In other words, $PHLX Semiconductor Index (.SOX.US)$ has shown a modest tendency to rebound shortly after breaking below its 250-day average, but that alone does not confirm a durable bottom.
What Comes Next?
The immediate focus shifts to $Anthropic (ANT.US)$ 's anticipated IPO and $NVIDIA (NVDA.US)$ 's November 17 earnings. Investors will be looking for confirmation that hyperscaler spending and AI chip demand remain strong.
However, data center financing, power availability and tighter global AI chip export controls remain unresolved risks.
Monday's rally has eased the immediate regulatory panic, but whether this marks the beginning of a sustained semiconductor recovery remains an open question.
